'''E-One Moli Energy''' Corp. is a Taiwanese manufacturer of [[lithium-ion battery|lithium-ion batteries]]. It was founded in 1998, and focused on producing high-capacity energy cells for notebook computers, high-end electronics, and networking communication devices under the "'''Molicel'''" brand.

In 2004, it partnered with [[Milwaukee Electric Tool]] to develop a high-energy power cell for cordless power tools, with its first power tool model introduced in 2005. It has also provided batteries to [[Ford Motor Company|Ford]] for electric cars, and in 2008, became the first qualified battery supplier for [[BMW MINI E]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.molicel.com/hq/about/aboutus1.html |title=Molicel-E-One Moli Energy Corp-Company Profile |accessdate=2010-12-25}}</ref>

Its E-One Moli Energy (Canada) Limited division has a facility in [[Maple Ridge, British Columbia]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.molicel.com/ca/ |title=Molicel - Rechargeable Lithium-Ion Batteries |accessdate=2010-12-25}}</ref> On November 16, 2023, E-One Moli announced that it will be investing $796 million in a manufacturing plant in Western Canada that will make lithium cells, though this was suspended on November 22, 2024. The new plant is expected to create 450 high-skills jobs with production of the batteries expected to start in 2028.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Taiwan battery maker to build $800m plant in Canada |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Business/Companies/Taiwan-battery-maker-to-build-800m-plant-in-Canada |access-date=2023-11-16 |website=Nikkei Asia |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=$1 billion expansion of B.C. lithium-ion battery factory on hold |url=https://vancouversun.com/news/maple-ridge-lithium-ion-battery-factory-expansion-on-hold |access-date=2024-12-21 |website=Vancouver Sun |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== History ==
The history of E-One Moli Energy goes back to Moli Energy Ltd., the Canadian pioneer of [[rechargeable lithium metal battery|rechargeable lithium battery]] technology, founded in 1977 in the [[Greater Vancouver]] suburb of [[Burnaby]] by the University of British Columbia and Teck Mining Corp., with Teck's then-chairman Dr. Norman Keevil Sr. as the lead investor.<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://electricautonomy.ca/2020/09/18/moli-energy-lithium-battery-technology/ |title=New lessons from the epic story of Moli Energy, the Canadian pioneer of rechargeable lithium battery technology |journal=Electric Autonomy Canada|author = Emma Jarratt|publisher=ArcAscent Inc. |date=2020-09-18 |access-date=2021-05-09  |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201005034041/https://electricautonomy.ca/2020/09/18/moli-energy-lithium-battery-technology/ |archive-date=2020-10-05 }}</ref> Moli Energy went into receivership after a cell-phone battery produced by the company caught fire in 1989, resulting in its sales being halted and tens of thousands of phones getting recalled.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=2020-09-18|title=The epic story of Moli Energy, pioneer of the rechargeable lithium battery|url=https://electricautonomy.ca/2020/09/18/moli-energy-lithium-battery-technology/|access-date=2021-12-11|website=Electric Autonomy Canada|language=en-CA}}</ref> The failure of Moli's battery technology caused a shift towards safer [[Intercalation (chemistry)|intercalation]] electrode materials.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Xie|first1=Jing|last2=Lu|first2=Yi-Chun|date=2020-05-19|title=A retrospective on lithium-ion batteries|journal=Nature Communications|language=en|volume=11|issue=1|pages=2499|doi=10.1038/s41467-020-16259-9|pmid=32427837 |pmc=7237495 |bibcode=2020NatCo..11.2499X |s2cid=218682825 |issn=2041-1723|doi-access=free}}</ref>

The company was then acquired by "a consortium of Japanese tech companies" for CA$5 million in a deal with the [[British Columbia]] government.   The deal was criticized for being far below the value of Moli's patents. In 1994, the company became Nippon Moli Energy Corp., and in 1997, it became NEC Moli Energy Corp. In 1998, it merged with Taiwanese E-One Technology, forming the current E-One Moli Energy Corp.<ref name=":0" />

On July 14, 2025, a fire broke out at a Molicel manufacturing plant in [[Kaohsiung]], originating in a warehouse containing semi-complete batteries. 12 workers and 3 firefighters were injured.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Scanlan |first1=Sean |title=Kaohsiung battery factory fire sends 15 to hospital {{!}} Taiwan News {{!}} Jul. 14, 2025 10:07 |url=https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/news/6155044 |website=taiwannews.com.tw |access-date=2 March 2026 |language=en |date=14 July 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Wang |first1=Lisa |title=Fifteen injured in TCC battery factory blaze - Taipei Times |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/biz/archives/2025/07/15/2003840289 |website=www.taipeitimes.com |access-date=2 March 2026 |date=15 July 2025}}</ref> The incident costed Molicel an estimate of NT$5 billion ($154.5 million USD) in damages.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Yang |first1=Carol |title=Molicel to shift production to Tainan after Kaohsiung battery plant fire {{!}} Taiwan News {{!}} Jul. 17, 2025 10:46 |url=https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/news/6157873 |website=taiwannews.com.tw |access-date=2 March 2026 |language=en |date=17 July 2025}}</ref>
